title: Intelligence & testing
examples: What are the main theories of intelligence?
How do we know if an IQ test is actually measuring intelligence?
What is the difference between validity and reliability in testing?

explain.say: We will start by looking at some major theories of intelligence.
Next, we need to understand what makes a test good. This is called validity.
Reliability means the test gives consistent results over time.
A test can be reliable but not valid, or even valid but not reliable.
In everyday life, think about a bathroom scale measuring weight.
A common mistake is assuming that a test that is easy to give is always good.

draw.text: Easy test does not mean good test

faq.q: What is the difference between general intelligence and multiple intelligences?
faq.a: General intelligence suggests one core ability, while multiple intelligences suggests several separate skills.
asks: Does everyone have one type of intelligence?
Is 'g' the only way to measure smarts?

faq.q: If a test is reliable, does that mean it is accurate?
faq.a: No, reliability only means it is consistent. A consistent wrong answer is still wrong.
asks: Can a test be consistent but wrong?

faq.q: How do psychologists test for validity?
faq.a: They test validity by seeing if the test scores correlate with other known measures of the skill.
asks: What links a test to real-world ability?
How do we prove a test works?

faq.a: They are tools, and like all tools, they have limitations and need careful interpretation.
asks: Are IQ scores the only measure of intelligence?
Do modern tests cover more than just book smarts?

faq.a: It is the field that deals with the theory and technique of psychological measurement.
asks: What is the science of testing?

facts: Spearman proposed the 'g' factor for general intelligence.
Validity refers to whether a test measures what it intends to measure.
Reliability refers to the consistency of test scores over time.
Gardner's theory suggests multiple, distinct intelligences exist.

quiz.say: A student takes an exam on algebra and scores highly, but later fails a practical algebra task.

options.show: The student is not intelligent enough.
options.say: The student is not intelligent enough.

options.show: The test might lack content validity.
options.say: The test might lack content validity.

quiz.why: Content validity means the test covers all necessary parts of the subject matter.

wrong.0: This is too vague; the issue is specific to what the test covers.
wrong.1: Intelligence is complex and not solely measured by one test.
wrong.3: Unreliable suggests the score would change randomly, which is not the main issue here.

quiz.say: A student takes a mood quiz three times in a row and gets nearly the exact same score each time.

options.show: The student has a stable mood.
options.say: The student has a stable mood.

quiz.why: Consistency across multiple administrations is the definition of reliability.

wrong.0: Consistency does not guarantee that the test is measuring the right thing.
wrong.1: While it suggests stability, the test itself is what is being evaluated for consistency.
wrong.2: The score's consistency relates to measurement stability, not difficulty level.

quiz.say: If a test is designed to measure reading comprehension, but it only uses vocabulary multiple-choice questions, what is the primary concern?

options.show: It is too simple for the students.
options.say: It is too simple for the students.

quiz.why: Construct validity checks if the test measures the underlying theoretical concept, like comprehension.

wrong.1: We cannot assume unreliability just because the format is too narrow.
wrong.2: Simplicity is a separate issue from whether the test measures the correct skill.
wrong.3: While true, 'lacking construct validity' is the formal psychological term for this limitation.
